lesson.title: A Wider Net: The ICD's Global Approach
lesson.summary: The ICD, the International Classification of Diseases, is published by the World Health Organization and is the classification system most widely used internationally, covering all health conditions, physical and mental, within a single global framework.
lesson.body:
While the DSM was built specifically for mental disorders and is centered on use within the United States, the ICD comes from a different origin. Published by the World Health Organization, it is designed to classify every health condition, physical illness, injury, and cause of death, not only psychological disorders. Mental and behavioral disorders make up one section within this much larger, more general system.

The current edition is the ICD-11, which came into effect in 2022 after adoption by World Health Organization member states. Because the ICD is meant to serve as a common reference for health statistics worldwide, tracking disease prevalence, causes of death, and health system planning across many countries with very different health systems, it is the classification system used more broadly around the globe, whereas the DSM's use is concentrated within United States clinical practice, research, and insurance systems.

The DSM and ICD cover much of the same diagnostic territory, and the groups responsible for each manual coordinate to keep the two systems reasonably aligned. Many disorders share similar or nearly identical diagnostic concepts across both manuals, and recent editions were developed with an eye toward harmonizing codes between them. Even so, the two systems are not identical, and they differ in some diagnostic thresholds, categories, and organizational structure. A clinician working in a United States hospital, for instance, typically uses DSM criteria to make a diagnosis but still needs to record a corresponding ICD code for billing and reporting purposes, since the ICD also functions as the underlying medical coding system for health care administration in the United States.

Both systems are best understood as working tools built to operationalize a genuinely difficult conceptual problem, turning distress, dysfunction, deviance, and danger into specific, checkable criteria, rather than as final, perfect answers to what a psychological disorder objectively is. Both are also living documents, periodically revised as evidence and understanding continue to develop.
